terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Pipe orders into the tool with `cat orders/press-2.txt | node orders.js check`, which works in PowerShell too.

tasks.title: Read the files a line at a time
tasks.description:
Rewrite `readOrders(names)` in `src/input.js` so that it reads each file a line at a time.

- it gives each line of each file named, in the order the files were named, as `{ file, line, text }`: the name as typed, the number of the line in its own file from 1, and the line without its line break, `\r\n` included
- it reads a file in pieces, so a file far bigger than the memory the tool has is read anyway, and it keeps no more than the line it is on
- a file that cannot be read still ends in one line on standard error that names it, and exit code 2

The check runs `node orders.js count` on a file of about 20 MB with 16 MB of memory for the tool's data, runs `list` and `check` on files of its own, one saved with Windows line breaks, and calls `readOrders` with two files of its own.
nextSteps: Run `node make-year.js`, then `node --max-old-space-size=16 orders.js count orders/year.txt`, and read how it ends.
Read "Reading a line at a time" in the lesson.
Open each file as a stream, turn it into lines, and yield each line as it comes.
Run the count with 16 MB again, then delete `orders/year.txt`: Check copies your workspace.
hints: `readFile` holds the whole file in memory at once, and splitting it holds it twice. Collecting the lines in an array before giving them on does the same.

A read stream gives a file in pieces, and `createInterface` from `node:readline` turns pieces into lines. `crlfDelay: Infinity` makes `\r\n` one line break every time. A generator can `yield` inside `for await`.
`for await (const text of createInterface({ input: createReadStream(name), crlfDelay: Infinity })) yield { file: name, line: ++line, text }`, with `let line = 0` before the loop, for each name.

tasks.title: Read standard input when no file is named
tasks.description:
Let the orders come from standard input, so another program can pipe them in.

- with no file named, `readOrders` reads standard input instead, a line at a time
- a file named `-` stands for standard input, at its place among the files: `orders check press-1.txt - press-2.txt` reads press-1.txt, then standard input, then press-2.txt
- a line from standard input has `file: 'stdin'`
- when files are named and none of them is `-`, the tool never waits for standard input

The check pipes lines of its own into `node orders.js`, with no file, with `-` between two files, and with a file named while standard input stays open and nobody types.
nextSteps: Run `cat orders/press-2.txt | node orders.js check` and see that nothing is read today.
Decide the list of sources first: the names, or `-` alone when there are none.
For `-`, read lines from `process.stdin` the same way as from a file.
hints: Standard input is a stream like a read stream of a file, so the same way of turning it into lines works on it.
`names.length === 0 ? ['-'] : names` gives the list to go through. Only `-` should ever touch `process.stdin`, so a tool given files never waits on it.
`const input = name === '-' ? process.stdin : createReadStream(name)` and `const file = name === '-' ? 'stdin' : name`, then the same loop as task 1.

tasks.title: Stop quietly when the reader goes away
tasks.description:
Make the tool stop at once, and quietly, when whatever reads its output stops reading, as `| head -3` does after three lines.

- when standard output is closed by its reader, the tool ends straight away, even while more input is still coming
- it writes nothing to standard error about it, and ends with exit code 0: nothing went wrong in its own work

The check runs `list` on a long file and closes its end of standard output after three lines. Then it runs `list` reading standard input, closes its end after three lines, types more lines, and keeps standard input open: the tool must end by itself.
nextSteps: On Linux or macOS, run `node make-year.js`, then `node orders.js list orders/year.txt | head -3`.
Read "When the reader goes away" in the lesson.
Listen for the error standard output gives when its reader is gone.
End the tool there, and let any other error be thrown as before.
hints: Writing into a pipe nobody reads fails with the code `EPIPE`. `console.log` hides that failure, so the tool keeps working for nobody; a plain `process.stdout.write` without a listener stops with the error.
`process.stdout` is a stream, and a stream says it failed with an `error` event. Here the work is over, so stopping at once is right, and nothing is left to write.
At the top of `orders.js`: `process.stdout.on('error', (error) => { if (error.code === 'EPIPE') process.exit(0); throw error })`.
